analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a gun, expands background checks, bans assault weapons, and ends gun makers' liability protection.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2020 with three cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled federal gun law: everyone buying or owning a firearm or ammunition would need a federal license after safety training and a background check, private gun sales would require background checks through a licensed dealer, purchases of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines would be restricted, and untraceable 'ghost guns' would be banned. It would also let families ask a court to temporarily remove guns from someone at risk of violence, raise the purchase age to 21, impose a 7-day waiting period, require secure gun storage, make firearm trafficking a standalone crime, and strip gun manufacturers of the federal law that shields them from most lawsuits. It also included grant money for community violence intervention programs and government research on gun violence.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities affected by gun violence, survivors of domestic violence and stalking (the bill closes the 'dating partner' loophole and adds misdemeanor stalking convictions to the gun-prohibition list), and families seeking extreme risk protection orders. Community organizations would gain new federal grants for violence intervention, and researchers would gain funding long blocked by federal restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal license requirement to purchase or possess any firearm or ammunition, with safety training, background checks, and a 10-year renewal cycle [S2][S3].
Extends background checks to transfers between private parties, closing the loophole for gun-show and online sales [S2][S3].

Lets family or household members petition a federal court for an extreme risk protection order to temporarily remove firearms from someone posing a risk of violence, with notice, a hearing, and court-appointed counsel for those who cannot afford one [S3].
Closes the 'dating partner' loophole in the domestic-violence gun prohibition and adds misdemeanor stalking convictions to the list of disqualifying offenses [S3].
Restricts semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, bans ghost guns and silencers, and raises the minimum purchase age to 21 [S2][S3].
Removes the federal law shielding gun manufacturers and dealers from civil liability and lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for firearms for the first time [S2][S3].
Funds community violence intervention grant programs and research on gun violence prevention [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Current and prospective gun owners would pay license fees, complete safety training, observe a 7-day waiting period, and securely store weapons on penalty of civil fines or criminal charges. Gun manufacturers and dealers would bear new excise taxes, security and record-keeping requirements, inspections, exposure to lawsuits, and the end of the assault-weapon and silencer markets they now serve.

drawbacks.text: The license requirement covers possession of any firearm or ammunition, applies even to long guns, and includes an ATF petition process to deny licenses based on 'unsuitability' findings, which critics said raises due-process and administrative-burden concerns for law-abiding owners [S3].

The 7-day waiting period, minimum age of 21, and secure-storage penalties with possible 5-year prison terms impose real compliance costs and delays on gun owners, including rural and low-income owners, even for uses like hunting and target shooting that the bill only partially exempts [S3].

The assault-weapon and silencer bans would eliminate entire legal product lines for manufacturers and restrict choices for current owners, and the bill relied on a buy-back grant mechanism for existing weapons [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed squarely at reducing gun deaths—through licensing, universal background checks, extreme risk protection orders, and storage rules backed by research showing these measures work—while also funding prevention programs in hard-hit communities. The costs fall heavily on gun owners in fees, training, waiting periods, and compliance, and on an industry facing new taxes, liability, and lost product lines. The objection that a universal license-to-own regime is broad and administratively heavy is legitimate, and courts would likely have tested its due-process design; but the bill included notice, hearings, and appeal rights throughout. On balance it was a comprehensive public-safety measure whose costs were concentrated and whose benefits were diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on February 5, 2020, joined by three Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Markey, Menendez, and Booker [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

The bill would have been among the most sweeping federal gun measures ever introduced, touching licensing, background checks, assault weapons, dealer rules, industry liability, and funding for prevention research [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers kept their liability shield, excise tax rates, and current product lines, and gun owners were spared a federal licensing regime. Communities affected by gun violence got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety Act of 2020 on February 5, 2020.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and Republican conference, 53 of 100 senators
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill or any companion gun-licensing measure to the floor during the 116th Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun-rights groups
against.role: Firearm industry and owner advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive gun-control measures of this kind, including licensing, bans on commonly owned firearms, and changes to manufacturer liability.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by Democrats, and gun legislation in this era generally split by party, but the record here shows no floor action to measure.

industries.note: The bill would end their federal liability shield, let the Consumer Product Safety Commission regulate firearms for the first time, raise excise taxes, and ban assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, silencers, and ghost guns. Its death preserved those protections and markets.
Dealers would have faced mandatory security plans, employee background checks, inspections, expanded record-keeping, and license-verification duties. None of these took effect.

industries.industry: Community violence intervention organizations and gun violence researchers
industries.note: The bill would fund local violence-intervention programs and federal research on gun violence, areas that have gone long underfunded. Its death left that funding unprovided.
